transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Khan (Redwood AE), Lina Zhao (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Cobalt ML), Jon Reyes (Cobalt SRE), Elena Garcia (Cobalt ML Platform)

Summary:
High-priority technical deep-dive to triage an accuracy regression observed after moving to a hybrid int8/AWQ profile on Cobalt's on-prem cluster. Focus on layerwise sensitivity, KV cache staleness/warmup interactions, batching policies, and deployment differences in VPC/on-prem CUDA stacks. Agreed actions: run a layer-bisect, share failing prompts, and schedule hardware-profile session.

Topics:
- Layerwise quantization sensitivity (GPTQ vs AWQ)
- KV cache warmup / staleness causing context truncation or odd completions
- Batching and dynamic coalescing effects on latency and accuracy
- On-prem constraints (CUDA 12.1 vs 11.x, mixed-precision FP8 kernel availability)
- Fallback strategies and canary rollout config

Action items (captured): see metadata action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: okay hey everyone thanks for jumping on, I'm Samir from Redwood, i handle the AE side for you folks. quick roll call?
[00:07] Maya: yeah Maya here, ml eng, we've been dogfooding the quant stacks. thanks for doing this.
[00:11] Jon: Jon, SRE. we'll mostly be listening and correlating logs.
[00:14] Elena: Elena, I run the platform, excited to close this gap.
[00:18] Lina: Lina from Redwood infra team, i'll drive the technical bits, especially layerwise and kv stuff.
[00:23] Priya: Priya, solutions eng, i'll help run bisect passes with you after.

[00:31] Samir: quick context recap — Cobalt flipped from hosted int8 profile into a hybrid AWQ profile in your dedicated on-prem cluster around 2026-11-28 and since then you've seen a measurable drop in QA/accuracy on a subset of prompts, plus occasional latency spikes when cache misses occur. is that the short version?
[00:45] Maya: yeah that's right. we saw a 3.8% drop on our metrics for the multi-turn diagnostic suite, and then weird completions when we hit cold kv states.
[00:53] Jon: and the latency spiking tends to co-occur with bursts, maybe after idle periods.

[01:02] Lina: ok. couple of hypotheses we prepared: one is layerwise sensitivity where certain layers quantized with AWQ (or int8) produce distributional shifts; two is kv cache staleness/warmup — the cache prefix isn't being populated in the same order in canary runs so you get different attention activation sequences; three is batching/coalescing interacting with kv cache eviction and increasing effective context warmup time.
[01:30] Maya: can you explain the kv staleness bit again? we thought kv cache was just a perf thing.
[01:35] Lina: sure — in short, KV cache stores key/value activations per token per layer. when there's a mismatch in request routing or batching order — say you coalesce two streams but their prefix overlap isn't aligned — the warmup hits different attention indices and the cached representations at certain layers are stale relative to the model's expectation, that can change token probabilities. we sometimes see that manifest as halluc or context dropout. we call it "kay-vee staleness" in notes but it's the same idea.
[02:05] Maya: oh, we did notice the failures happen more after low-traffic periods, so maybe warmup is incomplete.

[02:15] Priya: also worth noting AWQ's per-channel quant scaling can amplify small discrepancies at certain layers, especially if that layer has high dynamic range. GPTQ tends to produce different rounding noise (and AWQ's asymmetric handling can bias logits subtly). our plan is a layerwise comparison to find the top 3 sensitive layers.

[02:40] Elena: one question — on-prem GPU drivers: our infra is on CUDA 11.8 and some nodes are still on 11.4 for legacy workloads, will that change the quant kernels behavior?
[02:50] Lina: yes slightly. FP8 kernels and some fused int8 paths we ship are tuned for 12.x kernels, but we maintain fallbacks. on 11.x you might hit a slower fallback path that changes scheduling, which can increase coalescing windows and make kv warmup worse. it's not a correctness change per se, but scheduling differences can surface the issue.

[03:12] Jon: got it. so scheduling differences => different batching boundaries => kv misalignment => accuracy difference.
[03:18] Samir: exactly. and we saw something like this in a past customer where switching the NIC driver and reducing socket queue length fixed the burst boundary behavior.

[03:30] [Speaker 4]: um i see a note that AWQ uses per-column scale with stochastic rounding option? is that correct?
[03:37] Lina: yes, AWQ can use stochastic rounding during the quantization pass which reduces bias but adds variance; in runtime we don't do stochastic rounding on the fly, it's baked into the quant tables produced in the post-training quant step. GPTQ uses a different solvers approach that tends to minimize squared error per-weight but can leave different residual structures.

[03:58] Maya: we ran a quick A/B between gptq-int8 baseline and AWQ and AWQ actually matched on the majority but failed on ~120 prompts. they're concentrated on follow-ups and list-generation tasks.
[04:12] Lina: that pattern suggests either layers responsible for long-term memory (middle transformer blocks) are sensitive or the kv cache misalignment hits multi-turn sequences.

[04:25] Priya: can we walk through the bisect plan? how do we produce the layer sensitivity matrix?
[04:30] Lina: we'll do a deterministic layer-swap experiment — take the float16 baseline, then progressively replace layer X with its quantized counterpart and run the eval suite. do that for GPTQ and AWQ variants and build delta matrices per-prompt. that gives us per-layer deltas and a ranking.

[04:52] Jon: how long will that take on our infra? we have a mix of A100 and older H100-ish nodes.
[04:58] Lina: on A100 with our compiled runtime it's about 3-5 minutes per full eval per quant profile; H100s are similar but watch out for fp8 kernel availability. worst case it's a day to go through all layers on both profiles. we can parallelize across nodes.

[05:12] Samir: important note — collect and include KV cache warmup traces (we have a tracing hook) so we can correlate cache hits per-layer with prompt failures. Maya, can you export that?
[05:19] Maya: yes i can. we'll include the trace and a sample of the failing prompts.

[05:24] [06:00] Lina: another angle: batching policy. you mentioned you use dynamic coalescing with a 15ms window?
[06:06] Maya: yes default is 15ms and burst mode raises to 40ms.
[06:10] Lina: that 40ms in bursts is the concern — larger windows tend to mix different conversation states and increase cache eviction lifetime. if a request sits longer waiting for coalesce, the ordering changes. we recommend testing with a stricter coalesce or per-customer routing during canary runs.

[06:28] Jon: but stricter coalesce means more RPC overhead and lower throughput, any guidance on the tradeoff?
[06:33] Priya: we usually measure token/sec vs 95p latency and find a knee — often going from 40ms to 20ms reduces spurious misalignments while only dropping throughput 5-8% under typical load.

[06:50] Maya: there's also a suspicion about cache eviction TTLs — maybe our nodes evict older KV entries too eagerly under memory pressure. could that cause hallucinations?
[06:59] Lina: yes, if you evict a portion of keys mid-context you essentially force recomputation or mismatched attention; you may see the model lose track of enumerated items or repeat. send memory pressure metrics.

[07:12] Elena: security question — when you ask for KV traces, are those sanitized? they may contain PHI.
[07:18] Samir: good call — we can provide a sanitized tracer. we have a hook that hashes tokens and keeps only timing metadata for us to triage. we'll share the scrubber and you can run it locally before uploading.

[07:28] [08:00] Maya: let's talk about fallback strategy in production. we don't want a full rollback every time.
[08:06] Lina: recommended approach: layer-gating + per-prompt canary. layer-gating — we keep quantized weights for most layers but switch back to fp16 for top sensitive layers if a prompt fails certain eval checks. That's a small perf hit but isolates accuracy-sensitive contexts. second is model variant routing: route enterprise high-cost flows to a fp16 replica while default goes to quantized.

[08:30] Jon: runtime complexity worries me. how do we handle scheduling of mixed-precision replicas under reserved capacity?
[08:36] Priya: our scheduler supports capacity pools with different instance types and autoscale triggers. You can reserve a small fp16 pool for degradations; Redwood's smart routing will failover based on SLOs and model quality checks. We can include that config in the canary doc.

[08:52] Maya: when you say "layer-gating" is that static at deploy time or dynamic at request time?
[08:58] Lina: either — static is easier (deploy a mixed-weight artifact), dynamic requires a quick instrumentation path that can swap weight pages or use a fallback inference path for a subset of layers. dynamic is more complex but has less perf overhead overall when failures are rare.

[09:12] [09:30] Samir: let's cover the regression-not-reproducible cases — some prompts fail sporadically in prod but pass in canary. Any ideas?
[09:38] Lina: two likely causes — non-deterministic kernels (RNG in stochastic rounding during quant table generation, or non-deterministic cuBLAS paths under different driver versions) and request ordering differences. ensure determinism flags and set sticky batch ordering during canary to replicate.

[09:58] Maya: do we have a concrete checklist for deterministic runs?
[10:01] Lina: yes — set deterministic RNG, pin libcudnn and driver versions, disable async warmup and set batch ordering to FIFO, and run with identical coalesce windows. We'll share that checklist.

[10:14] Priya: quick note on AWQ vs GPTQ: AWQ tends to be better for activation distribution preservation in high-dynamic layers but can be biased on tokens that rely on small negative logits; GPTQ minimizes MSE across weights and sometimes keeps rare-token behaviors. we'll quantify with per-prompt delta.

[10:34] [11:00] Jon: any known CVEs or security considerations with quant tables? are they safe to store?
[11:06] Samir: quant tables are just numeric tensors; from a security perspective treat them as model artifacts. If you need FIPS/KMS-backed storage we support that in Private. we'll add storage guidance to the checklist.

[11:20] Maya: what about retraining or fine-tuning to adapt to quant noise?
[11:25] Lina: fine-tuning small adapters or LoRA on quantized weights can help recover quality; however it increases ops. Sometimes a light calibration step (bias correction on sensitive layers) suffices. We'll test adapters as part of the bisect.

[11:40] Elena: timeline — when can we expect the layer-sensitivity report?
[11:44] Samir: Lina and Priya will run the bisect and aim to deliver results in 5 business days — so dec 14.

[11:51] Maya: last question: if we confirm the problem is kv warmup, is the fix mostly infra changes or runtime?
[11:58] Lina: both. infra changes (coalesce windows, NIC configs, driver pinning) can reduce exposure; runtime changes (stricter cache warmup, per-request warmup hints, or increasing initial cache TTL for long sessions) can fix at the software level. often we do both.

[12:12] Samir: great. quick recap and next steps — Samir: we'll share perf baseline CSV and canary config by 12/11; Lina: run layerwise GPTQ vs AWQ and share matrix by 12/14; Maya: export failing prompt set and kv traces (sanitized) by 12/12; schedule hardware-profile call week of 12/15.

[12:32] Maya: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[12:36] Jon: appreciate it.
[12:38] Lina: thanks, we'll follow up in email with links.
[12:42] Samir: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
